current_native_entry.title: Evaluating AGENTS.md: Are Repository-Level Context Files Helpful for Coding Agents?
key_claims: Current arXiv:2602.11988v3 reports no significant success effect for LLM-generated context files (p = .87 on SWE-bench and .37 on CTXbench). Developer-written files show an +2.4% average resolution-rate difference versus no file (p = .21, not significant), and outperform LLM-generated files (p = .038).

Authors report mean inference-cost increases of 20% and 23% for LLM-generated files on SWE-bench and CTXbench. Developer-written files increase CTXbench cost by about 19%; Table 6 gives p = .0126. These are scoped author results, not an EPYC cost prediction.
According to the authors’ trace analysis, both LLM-generated and developer-written context files increase testing and repository exploration in the evaluated agents and benchmarks.

Current v3 recommends specific additional instructions absent from existing documentation and rigorous evaluation before adoption. It does not establish a universal benefit from shortening context files.
results: CORRECTED 2026-08-20 against v2: no significant success-rate effect for LLM-generated context files (p=0.87 / p=0.37); developer-provided files +2.4%. The v1 reduction framing does not survive into the current version.
Evaluated across multiple coding agents and LLMs on SWE-bench and novel repository issues
techniques: Comparison of AI-generated vs human-written context files
current_native_entry.notes:
Critical finding for our agent architecture. If context files hurt performance, our thin-map approach (minimal shared policy + lean role overlays) may be optimal — but we should validate empirically. The 20%+ cost increase from verbose agentfiles directly threatens PromptForge mutations that add instructions. Actionable: (1) benchmark our agent files with/without on SWE-bench subset, (2) add instruction token budget tracking to autopilot eval tower, (3) consider a "minimal context" ablation in PromptForge experiments. The finding that broader exploration doesn't improve success rates challenges the assumption that more context = better agent performance.

current_native_entry.title: KernelBench: Can LLMs Write Efficient GPU Kernels?
key_claims: The paper-era benchmark has 250 tasks in three levels: 100 single operations, 100 operation sequences, and 50 architectures. Current upstream has 270 reference Python tasks in four levels, with counts 100/100/50/20.

fast_p is the fraction of ALL tasks with correct output and speedup strictly greater than p; its denominator includes incorrect tasks. fast_0 equals the correctness rate, and fast_1 counts correct tasks strictly faster than baseline (ties excluded). The paper reports five randomized correctness inputs, three warmup iterations, and 100 CUDA-event timing trials with coefficient of variation below 3%. Current library correctness defaults to one trial, while the main evaluation scripts default to five.

The paper reports one-shot o1 fast_1 values of 10/24/12% by level and aggregate capability below 20%. Non-reasoning models produce more than 70% incorrect kernels in total; execution failures are the most frequent failure mode, while all evaluated models also struggle with functional correctness.
The authors report CUDA at 0.073% of The Stack v1.2 and hypothesize that its scarcity helps explain poor kernel generation. The paper does not independently establish that causal explanation.

Table 1 reports cumulative best-of-ten-generation refinement with generation, execution, and profiling feedback: DeepSeek-R1 fast_1 rises from 12/36/2% to 43/72/18%. Repeated sampling raises DeepSeek-V3 Level 2 from 4% to 37% at k = 100. The hardware comparison changes Level-2 R1 fast_1 from 36% on L40S to 47% on A10G, an 11 percentage-point difference.
techniques: PyTorch-reference-to-CUDA kernel generation task (torch cpp_extension load_inline)
Random-input empirical correctness checking (5 inputs) as undecidable-equivalence heuristic
Wall-clock speedup vs torch eager AND torch.compile via torch.cuda.Event
Multi-turn iterative refinement with exec + profiling feedback; repeated sampling (k up to 100)
reported_results: Paper one-shot o1 fast_1: 10/24/12% across Levels 1/2/3.
Paper DeepSeek-R1 refinement: 12/36/2% to 43/72/18%; DeepSeek-V3 repeated sampling Level 2: 4% to 37% at k = 100.
Paper Level-2 R1 hardware comparison: 36% L40S versus 47% A10G (11 percentage points).
current_native_entry.amd_rocm_transferability: HIGH feasibility for a ROCm/HIP analog, largely DE-RISKED by an existing follow-up. The harness is PyTorch-based, NOT bespoke-CUDA tooling: tasks are torch.nn.Module references, kernels loaded via torch.cpp_extension.load_inline, correctness is allclose on 5 random inputs, timing is torch.cuda.Event. Under torch-ROCm, torch.cuda.Event and cpp_extension work against an MI210 (HIP aliases the cuda namespace), so the correctness+timing skeleton ports with minimal change. CUDA-specific and to re-author: the 250 reference TASKS embed inline CUDA C (examples only); any nvcc/ncu/PTX/tensor-core profiling assumptions need hipify/hipcc + rocprof/omniperf. CRUCIALLY KernelBench itself is CUDA/NVIDIA-only (L40S; names Triton/CUTLASS/ThunderKittens as future work, evaluates none; NO AMD/ROCm/HIP), BUT the follow-up MultiKernelBench (arXiv:2507.17773) already abstracts a modular per-platform backend and states adding an AMD/HIP or Triton backend is '<20 LoC'. Recommendation: do NOT rebuild KernelBench from scratch - fork MultiKernelBench, register a gfx90a/HIP backend (hipcc + rocprof + torch-ROCm), optionally pull robust-kbench (Sakana, 2509.14279) anti-reward-hacking hardening. This is the concrete ROCm-KernelBench analog the user wants, folding into intake-660's verify+profile harness.
current_native_entry.novelty_justification: High. First benchmark to systematically measure LLM GPU-kernel generation with a combined correctness+speedup metric (fast_p) over a tiered 250-task suite; established the genre (every later kernel-gen paper benchmarks against it). Not a duplicate (only incidental sub-bullets in intake-278/intake-660; no standalone entry).
current_native_entry.relevance_justification: High, via the AMD MI210 (gfx90a, 64GB, ~July 2026) lens. The user flagged we will likely need a ROCm analog of exactly this benchmark to close the verify+profile reward loop. fast_p, the L1/L2/L3 op->fusion->architecture tiering, the random-input correctness gate, and speedup-vs-torch baseline are directly portable design decisions, and give the measurement substrate for intake-660's harness. Lower-relevance caveat only: nothing actionable until the MI210 lands and torch-ROCm is up.
current_native_entry.verdict_justification: worth_investigating (not adopt_component yet). The benchmark is CUDA-only and not directly runnable on our hardware today. Actionable path: when the MI210 arrives, fork MultiKernelBench (2507.17773) + register a HIP/gfx90a backend (hipcc + rocprof + torch-ROCm) rather than rebuild, adopt KernelBench's fast_p + tiered-task design as the scoring contract for the intake-660 ROCm harness, with robust-kbench (2509.14279) hardening against reward-hacking. Escalates to adopt_patterns/adopt_component once the GPU lands.
contradicting_evidence: Reward-hacking susceptibility: 'kernels' that just call torch/cuBLAS (sidestepping authoring), no-op kernels reusing the reference output buffer, mis-placed stream sync measuring an artificially short window. The 5-random-input correctness check is exploitable (Sakana robust-kbench; deep-reinforce 'Hacks and Defenses').

Numerical instability / naive baselines: original KernelBench inflated capabilities via exploitable tasks and naive baselines; tiny-op launch overhead dominates timing. robust-kbench and 'Towards Robust Agentic CUDA Kernel Benchmarking' (2509.14279) address these.
Narrow/dated op coverage, operator-level single-GPU forward-pass only (no distributed, no backward in v1). MultiKernelBench (285 tasks, 14 categories) and KernelBench-X broaden coverage.
Cross-hardware non-generalization acknowledged IN the paper (>10% L2 variance) - a kernel fast on L40S is not guaranteed fast on MI210, so a native gfx90a backend (not score transfer) is mandatory.

Confirmation-bias note: contradicting evidence is abundant and specific (a whole 'robust' successor literature exists) - this is NOT a low-evidence case; the criticisms strengthen the case for building a hardened ROCm analog rather than cloning v1 verbatim.
current_native_entry.dive_corrections:
DIVE 2026-08-10 (research-intake Stage-2b). Five factual corrections; one is decision-relevant. (1) DECISION-RELEVANT: this entry's amd_rocm_transferability field asserts KernelBench is 'CUDA/NVIDIA-only ... NO AMD/ROCm/HIP'. That is now FALSE — upstream shipped a first-party HIP backend. It does NOT unblock us: the backend's AMD_ARCHS list excludes gfx90a and it requires ROCm >= 7.1 (we run 6.2.0-66), so the practical conclusion (fork a multi-platform harness, register a gfx90a backend) is unchanged — but the stated REASON was wrong and must not be re-quoted.

(2) Task count and tiering: 270 problems across 4 levels upstream, not the 250 across 3 levels recorded in key_claims. The recorded figure describes the paper-era snapshot; the entry did not say so.

(3) Lineage: the released sequence is v0 -> v0.1 -> v0.2. There is no 'v1'; references to 'KernelBench v1' elsewhere in this index and in handoff prose are to the paper, not to a release.

(4) The library's default is ONE correctness trial, not the 5 random inputs the paper describes. Any claim about the strength of the correctness gate must say which it means.

(5) The shipped input distribution is strictly non-negative. This matters for anything inheriting the harness: a non-negative input distribution is the enabling condition for a ReLU-identity shortcut, and it is why the negate transform is load-bearing rather than decorative (see rocm-verify-profile-backend.md RVP-C2-3 / RVP-T0-5).

current_native_entry.title: MultiKernelBench: A Multi-Platform Benchmark for Kernel Generation
key_claims: Authors describe 285 tasks in 14 functional categories and evaluate CUDA, AscendC, and Pallas. Current source includes additional named backends; this static review did not run them or independently establish the authors’ priority claim.

The source implements a shared Backend interface registered with @register_backend(name), with device, hardware-name, compilation, correctness, and timing methods, plus optional cleanup and cheating detection.

The paper’s fewer-than-20-line extensibility example concerns Triton, not a HIP port estimate. Current source includes CUDA, Triton, AscendC, Pallas, SYCL, TileLang-Ascend, Catlass, AscendC direct launch, and MUSA. No named HIP backend or HIP/ROCm/AMD text was found in the searched Python and Markdown tree; Triton inherits the CUDA backend.

The paper uses five random correctness inputs with atol = rtol = 1e-2. Current source defaults to five trials but uses 1e-4 tolerances; explicit grouped inputs override the trial count. Source paths implement event/synchronization timing and separate compilation, correctness, and speedup metrics.

Current v2 Table 4(b) reports Claude-Sonnet-4 greedy Pass@1 of 47.0/2.1/8.4% on CUDA/AscendC/Pallas, but DeepSeek-R1 reaches 52.6% on CUDA. This platform skew is an author result, not an MI210 pass-rate measurement or proof that a refinement loop is mandatory.

Authors report category-aware exemplar improvements, including 380% relative compilation gains and 200% relative rows on AscendC. Transfer to HIP is an untested hypothesis, and these correctness/compilation improvements do not establish runtime speedup.

On 200 KernelBench tasks, GPT-5.6 Sol with in-context examples reaches Pass@3 of 100% on Level 1 and 88% on Level 2; correctness generation is distinct from optimization speedup. current_native_entry.title: Mercury: A Code Efficiency Benchmark for Code Large Language Models
key_claims: The original Mercury repository has no license-named tracked file or licensing declaration found in the searched source files. The paper declares its dataset CC BY-NC 4.0 and asserts Fair Use. Its current advertised replacement, Mercury_Eval, declares MIT in the manifest and README but has no license file. These are source declarations, not an independent legal determination or a basis for rejecting every current Mercury harness.

The paper’s Beyond formula is clipped min-max linear interpolation, not an empirical percentile. Its limitations assume uniformly distributed runtimes while Figure 2 uses percentile wording. Current Mercury_Eval separately implements Beyond and actual percentile rank; the old repository’s numerator clamping also differs from the paper formula.

For the paper’s Beyond score, failed solutions and correct solutions at or above the slowest reference both receive zero. Separate Pass/status information preserves correctness distinctions. Current Mercury_Eval also reports status and percentile, and its aggregate averages passing scores rather than the paper’s all-sample denominator.

contradicting_evidence: THE PATCH CONTRADICTS THE PROJECT'S OWN RELEASE CLAIM. seccomp=unconfined on containers whose entire purpose is executing untrusted model-generated code removes the syscall-filtering layer that is the main hardening of a Docker sandbox. Resource limits (cpus, memory, gpu pinning) are present; syscall confinement is deliberately not.

current_native_entry.source_revision: arXiv v1 (submitted 2026-06-01; only version as of retrieval 2026-08-10). Comment field: 'Accepted at ISCA 2026 Workshop MLArchSys'. Primary category cs.LG. Sole affiliation Gimlet Labs Inc., San Francisco.
current_native_entry.novelty_justification: 'kforge|gimlet|2606.02963' over research/, handoffs/ and chapters -> ZERO hits. 'intel arc|b580|sycl|metal|b200' -> Metal/SYCL/CuTe DSL appear only in serving-runtime portability entries, never in a kernel-GENERATION context. 'GEAK|ARGUS|HipKittens|KernelBench|kernel agent' -> the full intake-660..679 cluster plus 947/960/967. Medium, not high: the two-agent generate + performance-analysis loop with compile/correctness feedback is thoroughly covered by intake-662, intake-674 and intake-967. What IS new: first entry to frame kernel GENERATION behind ONE synthesis interface spanning four vendors and six programming models, first to name Intel Arc/SYCL and Apple Metal as generation targets, and first in the cluster to report an end-to-end result against a production vendor runtime on a real model rather than KernelBench-only.
current_native_entry.relevance_justification: Topically it lands on agentic-rocm-kernel-authoring.md and autokernel-research-loop.md, but the commissioning premise ('may be the most directly applicable paper in the batch') is NOT borne out. AMD appears in exactly ONE sentence — 'For AMD GPUs, we support HIP and Triton.' — with zero experiments and no mention anywhere of MI300X, MI250, gfx942 or gfx90a. The two evaluated backends are NVIDIA B200 and Intel Arc B580. Where it DOES earn relevance is the measurement axis: its numbers are an unusually clean quantified instance of the wall-share discipline in autokernel-research-loop.md §9.4 and of the 'weight end-to-end over isolated-op' eval philosophy.
current_native_entry.credibility_justification: Workshop peer review +1 (ISCA 2026 Workshop MLArchSys; +1 rather than +2 because a workshop track is not main-conference review). Recency +1 (~2.3 months old). Major lab / known contributor 0 (sole affiliation is a small commercial startup; individual authors' standing not verified and not asserted). Commercial bias -1 (presents the authors' own commercial product framework, no code or artifact released, and NO aggregate correctness statistics for ANY platform, so the headline claims are unreproducible from the paper). Corroboration 0. Total 1 — the lowest in the batch.
current_native_entry.verdict_justification: adopt_patterns, and a thin one. NOT adopt_component: no statement of code release, no repository URL, no artifact-availability section, so there is nothing to adopt. NOT not_applicable: squarely in domain with transferable content. NOT superseded in the strict sense, but its central mechanism is out-competed INSIDE our own index — intake-967 (ARGUS) reports 99-104% of hand-optimised assembly on AMD MI300X with KernelBench L1 100% / L2 90%, and intake-674/678/960 are AMD-native with first-class gfx90a knowledge; against those, KForge's +2.12% end-to-end and unevaluated AMD support add no capability.
key_claims: KForge describes generation and performance-analysis agents alternating functional and optimization passes; case studies use Claude Opus 4.6 in high-effort mode.

The read paper describes within-task iterative refinement, saved per-iteration artifacts and auxiliary reference-code injection. It does not describe or ablate an automatically accumulated persistent cross-task skill memory; that absence in this paper does not establish that memory is impossible or absent from every implementation.

KForge describes optional cross-platform reference-code translation, but its two case studies do not isolate the causal benefit of that translation. Measured NVIDIA/Intel results establish those evaluated capabilities, not a transfer ablation; assertions about Kernel-Smith remain externally unverified here.
The framework claims four vendors and six programming models, including HIP/Triton for AMD. The read evaluation covers NVIDIA B200 and Intel Arc B580; no AMD experiment is reported in this paper.
Generation uses a Py Torch reference, task description and one-shot example; cross-platform translation can supply an existing accelerator implementation as reference (CUDA to Metal is the example).
The paper defines five execution states and numerical checks with datatype-dependent tolerances. Its case-study tables report timing rather than aggregate counts or pass rates for the five states.

The paper acknowledges numerical-test correctness limits, missing source for production kernels, and possible attenuation of isolated speedups in full models; its B200 case nevertheless measures a 2.12% end-to-end throughput gain over Tensor RT-LLM.
techniques: cross-platform translation via reference implementation supplied as prompt context
profiler-output interpretation by LLM (Nsight Systems, Xcode Instruments)
reported_results: NVIDIA B200, gpt-oss-20b micro-benchmarks: fused Add+RMSNorm 1.10x-1.13x; MoE finalize 1.06x-1.43x; Bias+RoPE+KV-update near parity 1.00x-1.02x.

NVIDIA B200 END-TO-END vs TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0rc9 (512 requests / 1024-token prefill / 8192-token decode / batch 8, 7 independent iterations): throughput 2601.55 -> 2656.61 tok/s (+2.12%); wall-clock 1612.24 -> 1578.82 s (-2.07%); run-to-run coefficient of variation below 0.1%.

Intel Arc B580, Triton kernels, 37 GEMM+tail-ops problems from KernelBench Level 2: 5.13x geometric-mean speedup over the FASTER of PyTorch eager and torch.compile, attributed primarily to operator fusion and mixed-precision execution.

THE NUMBER THE COMMISSION ASKED FOR DOES NOT EXIST. There is no correctness or compilation pass rate for ANY platform, hence no NVIDIA-vs-non-NVIDIA correctness delta. The five execution states are defined but never tabulated. There is also NO ablation or measurement of the cross-platform-translation strategy — it is described as a capability, never evaluated.

LLM used: Claude Opus 4.6 in high-effort mode drives BOTH agents in the case studies; the framework is described as model-agnostic. The 37-problem subset selection methodology is not disclosed and the paper gives no total count for KernelBench Level 2.
contradicting_evidence: SECONDARY-SOURCE OVERCLAIM, and material. Automated summary aggregators assert that KForge 'successfully leverages cross-platform knowledge transfer, where providing a reference implementation from one architecture substantially improves the quality of generated code for different hardware targets'. TWO INDEPENDENT FETCHES of the paper confirm it contains NO ablation, NO with/without comparison, and NO numbers for this strategy — only a one-sentence capability description. Anyone citing 'KForge showed cross-platform knowledge transfer works' would be citing an aggregator, not the paper. Flagged because this is precisely the fabricated-citation failure mode the intake rules warn about, and because the commissioned question is exactly what that aggregator sentence appears to answer and the paper does not.

SELF-ACKNOWLEDGED and visible in their own data: the Table I -> Table II gap (per-kernel 1.06x-1.43x -> +2.12% end-to-end) is the paper's own 'isolated speedups do not always translate' limitation quantified.

STRUCTURAL: with no per-platform pass rates, no execution-state counts, no code release, and an undisclosed selection rule for the 37 problems, the two headline numbers are not independently checkable. The 5.13x in particular is a geometric mean over a self-selected subset.
No independent replication, rebuttal or failed reproduction surfaced in a bounded search (provisional — the paper is ~10 weeks old and only v1 exists).

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L23 (Entire paper body §§I–VI and Tables I–III; references statically scanned)
claim_anchors.quote: Production inference increasingly targets a heterogeneous mix of accelerators. Agentic pipelines interleave reasoning, tool calls, and multi-agent coordination, each with distinct compute and memory profiles. For optimal efficiency, each stage should run on the accelerator best suited to it. This creates a systems challenge: each pipeline now requires high-performance kernels across a growing set of hardware backends and programming models. Writing these kernels by hand is time-consuming, demands deep low-level expertise, and does not scale as kernel complexity grows. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been leveraged for automatic kernel generation, but challenges in low-level code generation and cross-backend generalization persist. We present KForge, a cross-platform framework built around an iterative refinement loop driven by two collaborating LLM-based agents: a generation agent that produces and progressively refines kernels using compilation and correctness feedback, and a performance-analysis agent that interprets profiling data, from programmatic APIs to GUI-based tools, and emits recommendations that steer the next round of synthesis. The loop alternates between functional passes, which drive a candidate to correctness, and optimization passes, which close the performance gap to hand-tuned baselines. We evaluate KForge on two backends with very different baseline reference availability. On NVIDIA B200, KForge achieves a 2.12% improvement in end-to-end throughput compared to TensorRT-LLM on the gpt-oss-20b inference speed benchmark. On Intel Arc B580, KForge generates Triton kernels achieving a 5.13 × \times geometric mean speedup over the faster of PyTorch eager and torch.compile on 37 GEMM + tail-ops workloads from KernelBench Level 2, primarily via operator fusion and mixed-precision execution.

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L79 (Entire paper body §§I–VI and Tables I–III; references statically scanned)
claim_anchors.quote: Structured artifacts for reproducibility. Prompts, model responses, generated candidates, evaluation results, and profiling outputs are saved per model and per iteration, making experiments easier to inspect and reproduce.

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L49 (Entire paper body §§I–VI and Tables I–III; references statically scanned)
claim_anchors.quote: Cross-platform translation. When a functional implementation already exists for one accelerator, it can be provided to the model as a reference, enabling cross-platform translation. For example, when generating Metal kernels, the prompt may include the corresponding CUDA implementation. This is particularly useful when the target backend lacks training data coverage.

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L44 (Entire paper body §§I–VI and Tables I–III; references statically scanned)
claim_anchors.quote: KForge is a multi-stage autonomous program synthesis framework, illustrated in Figure 1 . It supports iterative refinement, single-shot program synthesis, as well as repetitive sampling, where the mode of operation is directed by prompt construction. It is designed as a cross-platform framework and currently supports a diverse set of hardware targets, spanning four vendors and six programming models with varying levels of abstraction, visualized in Figure 2 . For NVIDIA GPUs, we generate kernels in CUDA, Triton, and CuTe DSL, covering both low-level hand-tuned and higher-level abstractions. For AMD GPUs, we support HIP and Triton. For Intel Arc GPUs, we target SYCL and Triton. For Apple silicon, we generate Metal kernels. KForge is also model-agnostic; the underlying LLM is selected through a model registry, allowing users to plug in any model without changes to the synthesis pipeline.

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L53 (Entire paper body §§I–VI and Tables I–III; references statically scanned)
claim_anchors.quote: We follow a task definition similar to that in [ 18 ] . Specifically, we treat the LLM as a function F : ( p ) ↦ k F:(p)\mapsto k that receives a text prompt p ∈ 𝒯 p\in\mathcal{T} as input and returns the generated code k ∈ 𝒯 k\in\mathcal{T} . The generated code is expected to contain a kernel program, a kernel scheduling code, a JIT-library compilation code, and a PyTorch model class NewModel(nn.Module) with a def forward(self, *inputs) method that implements the module’s forward pass. We use the Jinja2 template engine to parameterize the prompts. The default prompt p p contains a high-level task description, a one-shot example (a PyTorch implementation paired with its corresponding target-accelerator implementation), an input problem in PyTorch, and a task description in natural language.

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L59 (Entire paper body §§I–VI and Tables I–III; references statically scanned)
claim_anchors.quote: The proposed execution flow defines a closed feedback loop, with information that is either helpful in recovering from failures or allows the model to optimize a functionally correct implementation to achieve speedup. After every generation-evaluation iteration, we save detailed logs for each workload. We focus on five possible execution states:

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L118 (Entire paper body §§I–VI and Tables I–III; references statically scanned)
claim_anchors.quote: Beyond these, we highlight three research directions. First, the case studies in this paper rely on a source-level reference implementation to seed the generate-refine loop, but many production kernels, such as fused attention, GEMM-with-activation cubins, and vendor BLAS, ship without source code. Synthesizing kernels from a behavioral specification alone, with correctness checked against the closed-source binary, is a harder regime that we plan to explore. Second, KForge currently produces source-level kernels in programming models such as CUDA C++ and Triton. Targeting a low-level virtual ISA such as PTX would unlock optimizations that source-level programming models cannot express, at the cost of portability and a more challenging synthesis problem. Third, isolated kernel speedups do not always translate to end-to-end gains, since a faster kernel can shift register and shared-memory pressure or perturb the autotuner’s selections for neighboring kernels. We aim to extend KForge to jointly optimize kernels within larger architectural components, such as attention or MoE MLP blocks, focusing on the entire block rather than optimizing each kernel independently. Finally, as agents become more capable of long-horizon reasoning, these directions can be further augmented by leveraging the recent advances in autonomous agentic approaches.
generation failure — typical reasons: network error, model output does not contain workload’s code.
compilation failure — the generated result contains workload’s code, but fails to compile.
runtime error — the workload’s code compiles but fails at runtime, typically caused by segmentation faults or program abort.
numerical or shape mismatch — call to NewModel.forward returns tensors, but they mismatch in tensor shapes or expected values, or both.
correct — call to NewModel.forward returns tensors that match expected outputs both in shapes and numerically.

Several directions extend KForge beyond the scope of this paper. The current implementation targets PyTorch as the source Deep Learning framework and verifies correctness through numerical tests with datatype-dependent tolerances. Broader framework coverage, such as JAX, and more rigorous verification approaches, such as differential testing across diverse input distributions or formal equivalence checking, would extend the system’s applicability and strengthen confidence in LLM-generated kernels.

current_native_entry.title: GrepSeek: Training Search Agents for Direct Corpus Interaction
key_claims: DCI treats the raw corpus as an environment and uses executable shell commands without a learned document-retrieval index. Current v 2 provides SPCS without embedding indexing and optional PACE with a precomputed 2.8 GB auxiliary structure; no index of any kind overstates the whole system.

Current v 2 reports macro-average 0.5226 across eight benchmarks (seven token-F1 plus Browse Comp-Plus judged accuracy), best on five, and author-reported p<0.05 versus best dense baseline. Historical v 1 reports micro-average F1 0.5691 and four wins across seven benchmarks.
Current v 2 reports particularly strong gains on multi-hop Hotpot QA,2 Wiki,Mu Si Que and Browse Comp-Plus; the single-hop NQ result also improves, so benefit is not exclusively multi-hop.
Current v 2 retains Pop QA F1 0.4861 versus best-baseline 0.5101 and reports a statistically significant decrease; Trivia QA and Bamboogle also lose without reported significance.

Current v 2 reports raw corpus 14 GB for SPCS,16.8 GB including PACE auxiliary structure, versus retrieval structures 70 GB(E5)/221 GB(Qwen 3-4 B); figure labels memory footprint RAM. Setup is about 1 minute CPU for SPCS or 21 minutes for PACE, versus 3.2/62.4 A100-GPU-hours for embeddings; zero setup is inaccurate.

The source claims byte-exact equivalence and up to 7.6 x retrieval speedup for supported sharded shell pipelines with deterministic merges and sequential fallback. This is an author implementation/design assertion, not independent byte-equivalence testing performed here.
techniques: Two-stage training: answer-aware plus answer-blind cold-start data generation, then GRPO refinement
Tutor/planner distillation from a larger model into a compact agent
Constrained Unix action space (rg, grep, find, sed, awk, head, tail, cat, ls, wc, sort, cut, uniq, tr) - in practice dominated by rg and head
Sharded-parallel shell execution with byte-exact sequential equivalence as a correctness invariant
reported_results: v2 Table1: macro0.5226,5/8 benchmark wins;7 F1 datasets plus BrowseComp-Plus judged accuracy; p<0.05 author report
v1 Table1 (historical, disk re-read): microF1 0.5691,4/7 wins
PopQA0.4861 below best0.5101; statistically significant author report
Figure4: SPCS14GB corpus,P ACE16.8GB, E5/Qwen retrieval structures70/221GB; RAM footprint caption
SPCS setup~1 CPU minute; PACE~21CPU minutes; dense embeddings3.2/62.4A100hours
SPCS latency5.39s(1shard) to0.71s(32),7.6x author report; SPCS end-to-end8.67s vsE5 4.77s
current_native_entry.novelty_justification: High - it inverts the standing RAG assumption. The corpus IS the environment and the retriever is a trained shell-command policy; the pre-computed index is DELETED rather than improved. Dedup clean: the id appears once inside intake-1222 referenced_arxiv_ids and the name once in its prose; no entry existed. NOTE a predecessor stakes the same direct-corpus-interaction claim (arXiv 2605.05242), so the paradigm is not solely this paper - a fair reading should check whether the delta is the TRAINING RECIPE rather than the idea.
current_native_entry.relevance_justification: High and entirely HARDWARE-INDEPENDENT - this is a falsifiable claim about OUR retrieval design, not someone else. We run a ColBERT-backed kb-search over wiki/handoffs/research/progress/docs plus a GitNexus graph. Two reasons it lands harder than usual: their corpus is 21M docs / 14 GB, roughly THREE ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE larger than our markdown KB, and the grep advantage grows as the index amortisation argument weakens - on a corpus our size the index barely pays for itself; and their agent backbone is Qwen3.5-9B with a Qwen3.5-27B tutor, and WE ALREADY SERVE the 27B. COUNTERWEIGHT: their stated failure mode (surface-form variation, no semantic ranking, brittleness to spelling) is precisely where our KB is WORST - our corpus is full of synonymous governance jargon.
current_native_entry.credibility_justification: credibility 5/6. Arithmetic: base 2 arXiv preprint; +1 strong retrieval-research provenance (UMass CIIR - Zamani and Diaz are established IR researchers, not an LLM-hype lab); +1 honest and broad baselines - BM25, E5-110M, Qwen3-Embedding-4B, IRCoT, Search-O1, rejection sampling, and Search-R1 with the SAME retrievers, so not a strawman; +1 statistical significance reported and its OWN LOSSES reported (PopQA significant degradation, 3 of 7 benchmarks not best); +1 code released, CC BY 4.0; -1 v1 preprint with no independent replication, and the cost accounting favours the method by excluding agent GPU time from the headline while counting index-build A100-hours against the baselines.
current_native_entry.verdict_justification: worth_investigating rather than adopt_patterns, and the distinction is deliberate: the claim is cheap to TEST on our own corpus and expensive to adopt on faith. A four-arm A/B (ColBERT / untrained-rg / hybrid / GitNexus) over a pinned 40-60 question set stratified by hop-count and synonym-load is roughly one day with no GPU contention, and it either kills or justifies the line. Adopting before that would be adopting a Wikipedia-scale result on a corpus three orders of magnitude smaller, where the mechanism that produces the result (index amortisation) works differently.
contradicting_evidence: Their own PopQA result: statistically significant DEGRADATION on single-hop entity-centric QA.
Latency is 1.4-1.8x worse per query end-to-end - though dominated by LLM generation, not tool execution, so the index is not buying much latency either.

Their stated limitations - brittleness to spelling variation and diacritics, matches returned in FILE ORDER with no relevance ranking, overloaded keywords - map directly onto our KB weakest axis: heavy synonymous governance vocabulary, and at least one term ("duty cycle") already means two unrelated things in our corpus.
A predecessor (arXiv 2605.05242) stakes the same direct-corpus-interaction claim, so the paradigm is not solely this paper.
current_native_entry.amd_rocm_transferability: FULLY TRANSFERABLE - there is no GPU dependency in the claim at all. The retrieval mechanism is CPU/IO-bound ripgrep over text; the only GPU cost is serving the agent LLM, which we already do. Notably our 96-core EPYC 9655 is BETTER suited to the sharded-parallel engine than their setup - their 7.6x at 32 shards is not near our ceiling. claim_anchors.quote: Unlike RAG, which retrieves from a precomputed index, DCI searches the corpus directly by executing commands over millions of documents. 6 6 6 Our experiments use a 21M-passage Wikipedia corpus ( ∼ \sim 14GB). The agent uses tools such as rg , grep , sort , uniq , head , and tail . Since a trajectory may require multiple corpus scans, execution efficiency is critical. We apply semantics-preserving optimizations that reduce command latency while receiving outputs identical to execution over the original corpus. We use two complementary strategies.

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L143 (v2 abstract, introduction,§§2.1–2.2,3.1–3.2,Table1,Figure4 caption/text,AppendixC.3 algorithm and merge/fallback semantics; v1 abstract,§3.2,Table1 and efficiency discussion)
claim_anchors.quote: We compare GrepSeek against retrieval-augmented agentic search baselines in Table 1 . GrepSeek outperforms non-agentic approaches (Direct and RAG), untrained agents (IRCoT and Search-O1), and trained baselines (Rejection Sampling), with Search-R1 as the strongest competitor. Overall, GrepSeek achieves the best performance on 5 of 8 benchmarks, with statistically significant gains on 4 ( ↑ ), particularly on multi-hop tasks. These gains highlight the effectiveness of DCI for iterative evidence aggregation and entity-level precision, such as distinguishing subsidiaries from parent companies (Example E ) and avoiding name-collision errors (Example E ) in Appendix E . Performance is slightly lower on TriviaQA and Bamboogle without statistical significance, while PopQA is the only dataset with a significant drop ( ↓ ). These trade-offs reflect the lexical nature of GrepSeek . DCI is highly effective when queries contain strong textual anchors, including rare formulas (Example E ), distinctive phrasing (Example E ), and exact entity names (Example E ) in Appendix E . However, limited lexical overlap and form variation remain challenging: on PopQA, diacritics can prevent exact matches (Example E ), while overloaded keywords can cause rg to surface earlier but less authoritative matches because it lacks relevance ranking (Example E ). Dense retrievers are better suited to such cases by mapping lexical variants into a shared embedding space. Despite these limitations, GrepSeek achieves the strongest overall score ( 0.5226 0.5226 ), significantly outperforming the best dense retrieval baseline ( p < 0.05 p<0.05 ), showing that DCI provides a precise and effective alternative for open-domain QA and multi-hop reasoning.

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L86 (v2 abstract, introduction,§§2.1–2.2,3.1–3.2,Table1,Figure4 caption/text,AppendixC.3 algorithm and merge/fallback semantics; v1 abstract,§3.2,Table1 and efficiency discussion)
claim_anchors.quote: To evaluate GrepSeek , we conduct experiments across eight knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks: Natural Questions (NQ) ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ) , TriviaQA ( Joshi et al., 2017 ) , and PopQA ( Mallen et al., 2023 ) for single-hop QA in addition to HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) , 2WikiMultiHopQA ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , MuSiQue ( Trivedi et al., 2022 ) , Bamboogle ( Press et al., 2023 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2025 ) for multi-hop QA that need iterative evidence aggregation and reasoning. Experiments show that GrepSeek outperforms index-based RAG methods, untrained agentic frameworks, and even search agents optimized with RL to retrieve using dense and sparse retrievers. On average, GrepSeek achieves the best overall performance, with a 5.7 % 5.7\% statistically significant relative improvement over the strongest baseline, demonstrating DCI as a competitive and practical alternative to search agents that rely on index-based retrieval. Notably, it achieves the best performance on five out of eight benchmarks—NQ, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, and BrowseComp-Plus. The gains are pronounced on multi-hop tasks, where traditional retrieval systems frequently suffer from semantic conflation and entity ambiguity introduced by retrievers. We also show that our solutions are efficient for real-world applications. On a 14GB corpus containing 21 million documents, PACE reduces average retrieval latency from 5.39 5.39 to 0.07 0.07 seconds per query without sharding, yielding a 77 × 77\times speedup, at the cost of approximately 21 21 minutes of one-time preprocessing to construct its 2.8GB auxiliary structure. In contrast, our sharded-parallel execution requires essentially no additional preprocessing and reduces latency to 0.71 0.71 seconds with 32 32 shards, yielding a 7.6 × 7.6\times speedup. Thus, PACE is preferable when one-time preprocessing is affordable, while sharded execution provides substantial acceleration when additional preprocessing is undesirable. We will publicly release our codebase, the cold-start data, and model checkpoints. 1 1 1 Available at: https://github.com/alirezasalemi7/grepseek

claim_anchors.quote: Based on Table 1 , Search-R1 with E5 and Qwen3 embeddings are the strongest dense retrieval baselines. We compare their efficiency with our two DCI execution strategies—SPCS and PACE—in Figure 4 . All inference experiments use 32 CPU cores over 50 examples from each FlashRAG dataset (350 total), while dense-retriever indexing uses a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. As shown in Figure 4 (a), SPCS has an end-to-end latency of 8.67 8.67 s per query, including 0.81 0.81 s of tool execution, while PACE reduces tool execution to only 0.07 0.07 s and total latency to 7.93 7.93 s. In comparison, E5 and Qwen3-4B require 4.77 4.77 s and 6.07 6.07 s, respectively; the remaining DCI overhead is primarily due to longer LLM reasoning trajectories. Figure 4 (b–c) highlights the memory and preprocessing trade-offs. SPCS requires only the 14 14 GB raw corpus, while PACE requires 16.8 16.8 GB, including its compact auxiliary structure. In contrast, E5 and Qwen3-4B require 70 70 GB and 221 221 GB, respectively, to store their retrieval structures. SPCS requires approximately 1 1 minute of CPU wall-clock time for corpus setup, while constructing the PACE auxiliary structure takes approximately 21 21 minutes of CPU wall-clock time. Both avoid expensive embedding generation, which requires 3.2 3.2 and 62.4 62.4 A100 GPU-hours for E5 and Qwen3-4B, respectively. Finally, Figure 4 (d) compares search latency across execution strategies. SPCS scales from 5.39 5.39 s with one shard to 0.71 0.71 s with 32 shards, with diminishing gains at higher shard counts due to system-level bottlenecks such as memory bandwidth and merging overhead. PACE, even without sharding, reduces average search latency to 0.07 0.07 s by restricting execution to candidate documents rather than scanning the full corpus. These results show that the two optimizations are complementary: SPCS accelerates full-corpus execution through parallelism, whereas PACE avoids most of the scan altogether through candidate pruning.

claim_anchors.quote: To accelerate corpus interaction, we execute compatible shell pipelines in parallel over S S line-aligned corpus shards while preserving byte-exact equivalence with sequential execution (Algorithm 3 in Appendix C.3 ). The engine decomposes each pipeline, parallelizing it only when the first stage is a search operator ( rg or grep ) and all subsequent stages are shard-independent; otherwise, it falls back to sequential execution. Shard-local outputs are then reconstructed using operation-specific reductions: concatenation for stateless pipelines, local-plus-global truncation for head -n , summation for counts such as wc -l , and deterministic k k -way merging for sort / uniq pipelines. This improves throughput without changing the agent’s observations. Implementation details are provided in Appendix C.3 .

current_native_entry.title: GPU Forecasters: Language Models as Selective Surrogates for Kernel Runtime Optimization
key_claims: The paper formulates source-only candidate-versus-reference GPU performance forecasting as a probability distribution over eight ordinal speedup bins, described as logarithmic half-octave bins.
Selective use requires confidence to track forecast quality and permits deferral to real GPU measurement; calibration-shaped rewards are evaluated for this purpose.

All three RL rewards reduce ECE versus base, but all increase numeric forecast error. Brier improves recovered speedup(+2.06 pp at table budgets) and confidence-error monotonicity; CRPS reduces ECE while recovered speedup changes−1.05 pp. Calibration and accuracy must not be conflated.

In the six-task A100 search, the surrogate proposes four times as many candidates per parent and measures only the top quarter at equal GPU measurements per step. It wins three tasks, roughly matches Tri Mul, and loses two by about 5%/7%; a universal faster-kernel claim is unsupported.

The authors motivate coarse ordinal forecasting by the difficulty of fine numeric source-only speedup inference. This is a modeling rationale and observed nonzero forecast error, not a proof that all numeric inference is impossible.
techniques: 8-bin ordinal speedup classification with logarithmic half-octave spacing, NOT regression
Chain-of-reasoning before emitting a probability distribution over bins
Calibration-shaped RL rewards (Brier, CRPS) versus correctness-only
Selective prediction / deferral policy gated on forecast confidence
Input is reference source + candidate source + hardware spec - NO profiler counters required
reported_results: GPT-OSS20B Table1:82.88±3.85% recovered speedup across top1,5,10,25,50% budgetpoints; ECE0.441±0.011; forecast error0.643±0.011,three repeats
Table2 Brier: recovered+2.06pp,ECE−0.106,forecast error+0.130. Derived ECE0.335=0.441−0.106
Table2 CRPS: recovered−1.05pp,ECE−0.025,forecast error+0.100

current_native_entry.novelty_justification: Medium. LLM-as-performance-predictor is not new, but the SELECTIVE framing is the contribution - the surrogate must know when it is wrong and defer to hardware, with calibration (ECE, Brier, CRPS) treated as a first-class trained objective rather than an afterthought. The honest negative result, that fine-grained numeric speedups are not inferable and only ordinal bins are tractable, is itself a useful piece of novelty. Dedup clean: 2 hits, both inside intake-1222 prose; no entry existed.
current_native_entry.relevance_justification: Medium. It forecasts RELATIVE KERNEL SPEEDUP for search screening - so it bears on kernel selection INSIDE an authoring loop and on the C3/C5 rows, and NOT on capacity, throughput or serving performance in any form. Relevance is capped at medium by the single-GPU-family evaluation and, more importantly, by the fact that our GPU-measurement budget is NOT currently the binding constraint on kernel work - our binding constraints are one MI210 and a mostly-unbuilt evaluation backend. Optimising the search budget of a loop we have not yet made trustworthy is premature.
current_native_entry.credibility_justification: credibility 4/6. Arithmetic: base 2 arXiv preprint; +1 strong lab (Mohit Bansal group at UNC; Stengel-Eskin and Cho established); +1 code and a 12,388-kernel dataset released with the compute footprint disclosed (400M LLM tokens, 600 GPU-hours), CC BY 4.0; +1 reports calibration HONESTLY including bad numbers (ECE 0.441 base) and reports its own losses (baseline wins 2 of 6 tasks by 5-7%); -1 evaluated on NVIDIA A100 ONLY with NO cross-GPU transfer test, despite the released dataset containing three GPU types - the one experiment that would establish generality was available and not run.
current_native_entry.verdict_justification: adopt_patterns - the METHOD and the METRICS, explicitly not the trained artifact. ADOPT: ordinal log-half-octave bins instead of numeric speedup regression as our reward shape, because their negative result says numeric regression will not work and we should not spend a cycle rediscovering that; a calibration metric (ECE or Brier) as a first-class ACCEPTANCE GATE on any predictor we build; and an explicit DEFERRAL policy so a surrogate must escape to real gfx90a measurement. DECLINE the trained forecaster outright: it is A100-conditioned with zero transfer evidence, and a speedup bin predicted for A100 says nothing about gfx90a where memory hierarchy, LDS size and matrix-core shapes all differ.
contradicting_evidence: Baseline search BEATS the surrogate-enhanced search on 2 of 6 tasks by 5-7% - so the surrogate is not free; it can steer a search AWAY from the best kernel. Any adoption needs the equal-budget baseline arm run alongside, never a single-arm demo.
ECE 0.441 base is poor calibration in absolute terms, and even the Brier-trained 0.335 is not good - so the paper own selectivity thesis is only partly delivered.
Its own stated limitation contradicts a naive reading of the title: LLMs cannot forecast numeric runtime, only coarse ordinal bins.

SINGLE-VENDOR UNTRANSFERABILITY, and this is now a PATTERN rather than an incident: KernelPro (intake-1222), CudaForge (intake-662) and now this all evaluate on one NVIDIA family and ship artifacts that cannot cross to gfx90a. The recurring lesson - METHOD transfers, TRAINED ARTIFACT never does - is well enough evidenced that it should be stated once in the wiki rather than re-derived per intake.
current_native_entry.amd_rocm_transferability: TRAINED ARTIFACT: zero transfer - A100-only with no cross-GPU test performed, so a predicted bin carries no information about gfx90a. DATASET: zero direct transfer (CUDA/Triton kernels measured on NVIDIA) but usable as a STRUCTURAL TEMPLATE for a gfx90a dataset. METHOD AND METRICS: high transfer - ordinal binning, calibration-as-a-gate and the deferral policy are architecture-neutral design choices that would improve any predictor we build for C3. CHEAP FIRST PROBE if we ever want the surrogate: take the ~480-kernel eval protocol SHAPE but populate it from OUR gfx90a measurements, and check whether an off-the-shelf served model can rank-order two HIP kernels better than chance. One day, no training, and it either kills or justifies the line.

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L86 (Abstract,introduction,§§2–3.5,Tables1–2,Figure4–6 text/captions,AppendixB/E evaluation construction andTable3 bins)
claim_anchors.quote: Predicting an absolute runtime in seconds from source code alone is intractable, as it would require modeling compiler behavior, launch overheads, memory hierarchy effects, scheduling, resource occupancy, and other hardware-dependent execution details. We instead define the prediction target as the candidate’s speedup S i S_{i} relative to the reference, discretized into eight ordinal bins. We use logarithmic (half-octave) speedup bins rather than linearly spaced bins because the surrogate is forecasting from source code rather than executing the kernel. Fine-grained numeric speedups, such as distinguishing a 2 × 2\times improvement from a 3 × 3\times improvement, are difficult to infer reliably without running the kernel. Coarse factor-level judgments are more realistic: the model can estimate whether a candidate is much slower, near baseline, moderately faster, or much faster. These intervals make the forecast target meaningful and tractable while preserving the distinctions a kernel optimizer needs; the full bin table is provided in Table 3 . The surrogate emits a probability distribution over the eight bins:

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L78 (Abstract,introduction,§§2–3.5,Tables1–2,Figure4–6 text/captions,AppendixB/E evaluation construction andTable3 bins)
claim_anchors.quote: This paper makes five contributions. (1) We show that under the right prediction objective, LLMs achieve non-trivial accuracy in forecasting how a GPU responds to a candidate kernel . (2) We cast GPU forecasting as a selective prediction problem, in which the surrogate must report calibrated uncertainty so that downstream search can decide which predictions are reliable enough to act on. (3) We apply reinforcement learning to an open-weights surrogate and characterize how training shifts its ranking, calibration, and forecast quality. (4) We show that the surrogate improves end-to-end kernel search , finding faster kernels than an equal-GPU-budget baseline on most tasks by letting the search consider more candidates per measurement. (5) We build a reusable, multi-purpose collection of 12,388 LLM-generated GPU kernels with measured runtimes , spanning 118 problems, CUDA and Triton, three GPU types, and four generation methods, costing 400M LLM tokens and 600 GPU-hours. The full release supports broader work on GPU performance prediction, kernel search, and LLM-generated low-level code. More broadly, GPU surrogates connect kernel optimization to efforts to build neural simulators of complex physical and virtual systems [ 29 , 41 ] . The long-term promise of such models is not only faster prediction, but the ability to generate training data and support model-based optimization without querying the original system at every step. A surrogate offers higher throughput and lower per-query cost than a GPU, in exchange for forecast noise that calibrated uncertainty estimates can help manage.

claim_anchors.locator: source.txt:L131 (Abstract,introduction,§§2–3.5,Tables1–2,Figure4–6 text/captions,AppendixB/E evaluation construction andTable3 bins)
claim_anchors.quote: Table 2 compares each RL reward to the GPT-OSS-20B base. All three rewards improve calibration, but they differ in search utility: correctness-only training loses 1.29 1.29 % in speedup recovered, CRPS is roughly neutral, and Brier gains 2.06 2.06 %. The correctness reward only checks whether the argmax bin is correct, so it can improve exact-bin decisions while ignoring how useful the rest of the probability vector is. Brier and CRPS instead score the full distribution p i p_{i} . That matters for search because candidates are ranked by expected speedup, S ^ i = ∑ b p i , b ​ m b \hat{S}_{i}=\sum_{b}p_{i,b}m_{b} , not just by the argmax bin. A probability vector with informative mass across nearby bins can separate candidates that share the same predicted bin while a binary vector cannot. The tradeoff is that all trained variants increase forecast error. Forecast error uses only the argmax-bin representative m y ^ i m_{\hat{y}_{i}} , so it can worsen when training shifts the most likely bin even if the full distribution becomes better calibrated or more useful for ranking. Calibration is important here, as it affects decision-making about when to defer, which kernels to prioritize, and other actions which depend on the quality of the forecast distribution.

claim_anchors.quote: Predicting an absolute runtime in seconds from source code alone is intractable, as it would require modeling compiler behavior, launch overheads, memory hierarchy effects, scheduling, resource occupancy, and other hardware-dependent execution details. We instead define the prediction target as the candidate’s speedup S i S_{i} relative to the reference, discretized into eight ordinal bins. We use logarithmic (half-octave) speedup bins rather than linearly spaced bins because the surrogate is forecasting from source code rather than executing the kernel. Coarse factor-level judgments are more realistic: the model can estimate whether a candidate is much slower, near baseline, moderately faster, or much faster. current_native_entry.amd_rocm_transferability: ZERO AMD COVERAGE, VERIFIED NEGATIVE. Grep for AMD, ROCm, HIP, MI2xx, CDNA, gfx, wavefront over the full paper: NO HITS. The released corpus is equally NVIDIA-shaped (rocm/amd/cdna/wavefront x0 across 2 MB of skill text; cublas x27, cudnn x19, warp x207). The environment is CUDA-HARDCODED, not merely defaulted: correctness.py calls x.cuda(device=device) and torch.cuda.synchronize(device=device); the backend sets CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES and TORCH_USE_CUDA_DSA=1; the device map is cuda:{i}. WHAT MIGHT STILL RUN: a ROCm PyTorch build absorbs .cuda() and Triton has a gfx90a backend, so KernelGYM might execute on our MI210 - but nothing here has been exercised on AMD, the vendor-library skills map onto rocBLAS/MIOpen with different performance cliffs, and every verify_speedup is an NVIDIA measurement. BOUND THE CLAIM HONESTLY: any number we produce from this corpus on gfx90a is a RE-MEASUREMENT, never a transfer. A TRAIN-FREE PATH NEVERTHELESS EXISTS AND IS THE ACTIONABLE PART: the repo exposes skill injection as a runtime flag (SKILL_ENABLE, SKILL_LIBRARY_FILE) independent of training and can drive an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so a BM25-rerank-inject-execution-verify loop runs against any model we serve with zero training. THE PAPER NEVER MEASURES THAT CONFIGURATION, so its value is unknown.

DIRECT REBUTTAL for smaller/self-hosted models: arXiv 2512.17920 finds constraint compliance degrades substantially FASTER than semantic accuracy under compression, and smaller models violate constraints more readily at the same ratio (most pronounced at ~40-60% compression). Prompt compression is strongly task-dependent: up to 52% performance drops on classification vs minor degradation on TriviaQA/SAMSum (arXiv 2410.12388, 2604.02985). A single aggregate "no degradation" verdict cannot hold across task types.

Direction of effect is model-size-dependent in BOTH directions (arXiv 2603.13306: few-shot and CoT prompts REDUCE accuracy for tiny/small models). current_native_entry.title: RLPF - staged correctness-gated reward for RL code performance optimization
key_claims: RLPF is a separate study using a correctness-gated staged reward. This is related architectural evidence, not an empirical gate-versus-blend corroboration of intake-939; intake-939 was not re-read in this dive, so comparator authorship and evidence independence are not established here.
Every reward arm tested remains correctness-gated; there is no ungated or blended arm, so the study cannot show that gating beats blending.

The paper and official reward code set epsilon=0.05 above the wrong-output stage reward 0.10, so correct programs receive at least 0.15. This deliberately preserves positive reward for correct-but-slow outputs; any contrast with intake-939 is cross-entry and was not re-read in this dive.

The pre-correctness ladder orders extraction failure (-0.05), compile failure (0.00), runtime failure (+0.05), and wrong output (+0.10). This is a source-verified design, while applying it to EPYC is a proposal.
CGRE is correctness multiplied by clipped task-specific gap closure (baseline-to-candidate over baseline-to-reference), bounded to [0,1].
reported_results: Code-verified reward: R_succ=CGRE+0.16*FBR+0.10*RBR; incorrect cases use the stage reward; correct cases use max(stage reward for wrong output + epsilon, R_succ), epsilon=0.05.

One-seed, 306-task reported ablation point estimates: full RLPF 54.58 CRR / 14.97 Slow-CRR; w/o FBR 40.52; w/o RBR 39.87; w/o shaping 39.54; runtime-only (still gated) 37.91; RLVR correctness-only 50.00 CRR / 36.60 Slow-CRR. No confidence intervals; authors limit component-necessity inference.
At near-matched correctness, paper reports 36.6% Slow/CRR for correctness-only vs 15.0% for RLPF; paper transition counts yield McNemar p<0.0001.
The paper reports +34/-20 for its correctness comparison (McNemar p≈0.06); component ablation differences are only 1–2 tasks and do not establish component necessity.
Authors report 597 GPU-hours for the full run and roughly 4,000 GPU-hours for the study.
contradicting_evidence: PAPER/CODE DISCREPANCY - THE SMOKING GUN. Eq. 2 defines RBR = 1[T_c <= T_r]. Released reward.py applies an UNDOCUMENTED rbr_tolerance = 0.02 (t_model <= t_ref * 1.02), with a code comment attributing it to timing noise. The authors OBSERVED the hazard at the threshold, PATCHED IT WITH A 2% FUDGE, and did NOT report it. All published RBR figures carry 2% slack Eq. 2 does not state - a measured admission that their harness cannot resolve sub-2% differences, while CGRE, the headline metric, is a CONTINUOUS function of exactly those differences.

IT INHERITS THE TIMING HAZARD ALMOST COMPLETELY. Reward execution runs ON THE SAME BOX as 32B GRPO rollout generation; CUDA tasks timed on the TRAINING GPUs; no isolation, taskset, numactl, affinity or quiescing anywhere. Measure-ONCE during training. FRESH candidate timing against DISK-CACHED baseline timing with zero drift correction (PERFCODEBENCH_USE_BASE_REF_CACHE defaults TRUE, USE_CANDIDATE_CACHE defaults FALSE) - precisely the stored-vs-fresh comparison intake-939 affine recalibration exists to fix.

NON-INDEPENDENCE THE BRIEF DID NOT ANTICIPATE: PerfCodeBench IS THE AUTHORS OWN BENCHMARK - 7 of its 8 authors are also RLPF authors, including the same first author. RLPF trains on it, evaluates on it, and draws EVERY headline number from it. BOTH papers headline numbers rest on self-built, externally-unrun corpora.
NO LICENCE FILE. README: "A standalone license has not yet been added." Benchmark tasks are not in the repo. adopt_component is BLOCKED on this.
current_native_entry.novelty_justification: medium. The reward family is already characterized by intake-939; what is new is an independent group choosing the OPPOSITE gate form within it, plus two mechanisms 939 lacks entirely (the failure ladder and the continuous gap-closure form).
current_native_entry.relevance_justification: high. The pre-correctness failure ladder maps directly onto the MI210 kernel loop, where most candidates die before they can be timed and are currently all scored identically.
current_native_entry.verdict_justification: adopt_patterns, with adopt_component explicitly BLOCKED by the missing licence file and the absent benchmark tasks.

key_claims: TRACK, DO NOT ADOPT remains the posture pending licensed reuse terms and a relevant ROCm/HIP path.

PerfCodeBench v2 describes executable systems performance tasks with baseline and expert-optimized references, correctness oracles, and runtime targets; this makes it potentially relevant, not validated for MI210/ROCm.
It is materially closer to systems optimization than LeetCode-style tasks, but that does not establish architecture compatibility or a valid EPYC kernel measurement.

The public GitHub release overturns the old anonymous-review-only/unreleased assertion. The repo has no umbrella LICENSE/COPYING (GitHub license=null); its reviewed CUDA path is NVIDIA-toolkit oriented, with no HIP/ROCm route found. Paper v2 reports CUDA 128 vs 125 cuda_-prefixed directories in the pinned repo; the old 5.2% test-split claim is unsubstantiated in this version. Eight author overlaps with RLPF mean no independent corroboration.
reported_results: Paper v2 reports 1,854 executable performance tasks. Pinned repository snapshot has 1,854 top-level executable_tasks directories.
Pinned repository snapshot has 125 cuda_-prefixed directories; paper v2 Figure 1 reports CUDA 128. This is a version/snapshot discrepancy, not a verified test-split proportion.
Paper describes per-task fixed interfaces, baseline implementation, expert-optimized reference, correctness oracle, and harness.
contradicting_evidence: Every RLPF headline number is drawn from this benchmark, and 7 of its 8 authors are RLPF authors. It is a self-built, externally-unrun corpus - the same non-independence pattern the index has already flagged for the Mingzhe Du bloc and for FAIR own DMC-Optim.
current_native_entry.novelty_justification: medium. Systems-level performance tasks with paired baseline and expert reference are genuinely rare in this literature; everything else is competitive-programming or repo-level Python.
current_native_entry.relevance_justification: medium and conditional. If it were released under a licence and grew a ROCm path, it would be the closest published instrument to our own kernel work. Today the CUDA slice is 5.2% of the test split and nvcc-bound.
current_native_entry.verdict_justification: worth_investigating with an explicit DEFER: re-check in roughly 60 days for a release, a licence, and any ROCm/HIP path. Not not_applicable - the design is right; the availability is not.
recommended_actions: [review candidate] DEFER roughly 60 days. Named triggers for reopening: a public release with a licence, and any ROCm/HIP execution path.

current_native_entry.title: Rethinking Code Performance Benchmarks for LLMs - only 6.11% of "performant" reference implementations are significantly faster on the original tests
key_claims: This separate study provides related evidence about performance benchmarks, not an independent replication of intake-939: it measures per-task statistical significance after repeated runtime sampling, not robust CV/IQR or the CV≥0.3 duration-spread criterion. Comparator authorship and trace independence are not established by this current-paper read.

The paper re-evaluates 1,538 tasks from EffiBench (1,000), Enamel (164), EvalPerf (118), and Mercury (256), with 30 runs per implementation pair and per-task Mann–Whitney U testing. Retain the existing intake-972#1 dependency because Mercury supplies 256 denominator tasks; no independent re-read of intake-939 is claimed.

On the benchmark-provided original tests, authors report 94 of 1,538 implementations (6.11%) significantly faster than their canonical counterparts under per-task Mann–Whitney U at p<0.05. This is the original slot’s statistical-significance result, not duration spread or proof of an absence of optimization.

In a stratified manual sample of 308 non-significant comparisons, authors classify 209 code changes as plausibly performance-improving. These are potential improvements, not 209 experimentally verified speedups or proof that test workload alone caused every non-significant result.

Generated performance-oriented test suites reveal significant differences on 323 of 1,345 (24.01%) and 342 of 1,345 (25.43%) initially non-significant tasks. This is bounded author-reported evidence from four primarily Python function-level benchmarks, not an EPYC kernel result or a guarantee for other systems.
reported_results: Four benchmarks, 1,538 tasks, 30 repeats/task; 94/1,538 (6.11%) significantly faster on original benchmark tests at p<0.05.
In a stratified sample, 209/308 changes were judged plausibly performance-improving; this was not direct speedup verification.
Two generated performance-test suites revealed significant runtime differences on 323/1,345 (24.01%) and 342/1,345 (25.43%) initially non-significant tasks.
current_native_entry.novelty_justification: high. It is the only cross-benchmark audit in the corpus that re-runs four instruments at 30 reps and applies a statistical test to the reference implementations themselves.
current_native_entry.relevance_justification: high, and it settles a live question. It is the empirical reason our sealed SWE40/LCB tasks physically cannot carry a timing signal: their original correctness tests do not exercise the workload where the optimization lives.
current_native_entry.verdict_justification: adopt_patterns. Its finding is what we consume, not its harness.
recommended_actions: [review candidate] CITE as the independent corroboration of intake-939 duration-spread claim - different group, different method, same conclusion.

[review candidate] DECLINE adding an efficiency axis over our sealed SWE40/LCB tasks. Original correctness tests clear the duration-spread gate for at most 3.8% of problems, and this paper independently measures 6.11% significance on reference implementations. Our sealed tasks physically cannot carry a timing signal.

current_native_entry.title: MLEvolve - Monte Carlo GRAPH search with cross-branch reference edges for ML engineering agents (ID CORRECTION)
key_claims: MLEvolve is arXiv:2606.06473 (Du et al., 2026-06-04); arXiv:2606.11926 is a separate work, not re-read here.

Official OpenAI MLE-Bench README records MLEvolve / Gemini-3-Pro-Preview on 2026-02-14: Lite 80.30±1.52, Medium 57.89, High 42.22, All 61.33±1.33, 12h; source and grading reports marked available. The same mainline table also marks Leeroo source available, so MLEvolve is not the only top-10 source-available entry. Apache-2.0 is confirmed in current repo.

Paper Table 1 separately reports Gemini-3.1-Pro-preview, 12h, Lite 80.3 / Medium 64.0 / High 46.7 / All 65.3±0.8 over three seeds. Only Lite overlaps the older official row; 65.3 is paper-reported and not the verified 61.33 leaderboard score.

Paper lists H200, 21 vCPUs, 234 GB RAM. MLE-Bench recommends A10/36 vCPUs/440 GB as defaults but explicitly says they are not strict requirements; there is no demonstrated compute match, and the official row does not document exact hardware.

Paper/repo describe progressive graph search with cross-branch references, explore/exploit scheduling, retrospective/global memory, and separated planning/code generation. Current Apache-2.0 repo says CPU can be selected for memory embeddings only, while defaults/dependencies use CUDA and one GPU. EPYC kernel-search transfer remains untested.
techniques: Monte Carlo Graph Search with cross-branch reference edges
reported_results: Official board row, pre-freeze 2026-02-14: Lite 80.30±1.52, Medium 57.89, High 42.22, All 61.33±1.33, 12h; source and grading report marked available.
Paper-reported post-freeze, different backbone: Gemini-3.1-Pro-preview All 65.3±0.8; not the verified official-board result.
contradicting_evidence: DOES IT BEAT intake-940 (Frontis-MA1)? YES at matched WALL-CLOCK - 80.30 vs 71.21 Lite at 12h = 6 medal outcomes (9.09 pp), roughly 4x the entire Frontis-MA1 headline margin. NOT matched on COMPUTE: Frontis-MA1 ran on one RTX 4090 capped at 12 GB VRAM with a 35B open-weight backbone; MLEvolve on an H200 (141 GB) with a proprietary frontier backbone.

The correct statement: at matched wall-clock but ~12x GPU memory and a closed frontier model, the verified SOTA is 6 medal outcomes ahead of Frontis-MA1 best. Frontis-MA1 frontier-competitiveness claim must be scoped to its compute class - the paper does not scope it, and the omission is the defect.
current_native_entry.novelty_justification: medium. Graph search over tree search and cross-branch reference edges are the genuinely new mechanisms; the memory and planning structure are variations on patterns already indexed.
current_native_entry.relevance_justification: high. It is the verified comparator that intake-940 Table 11 omits, and MCGS with reference edges is directly applicable to the autopilot archive and the AutoKernel planner, both of which currently isolate branches.
current_native_entry.verdict_justification: adopt_patterns: Apache-2.0 and CUDA-optional, but specialized for Kaggle-style MLE program synthesis rather than anything in our serving path. The mechanisms transfer; the harness does not.
recommended_actions: [review candidate] ADD a ninth dive_correction to intake-940 naming this as the omitted verified comparator, with the compute-class scope qualifier attached.
[review candidate] CITE 61.33 All (leaderboard-verified) and NEVER 65.3 (self-reported on a different backbone, post-freeze).
[review candidate] EVALUATE cross-branch reference edges against our current branch-isolated archive designs.

current_native_entry.title: CTRL-ALT-DECEIT - sabotage and sandbagging by ML-engineering agents, and what a monitor can and cannot catch
key_claims: The paper observes sandbagging through small training subsets and small CNNs in ML-engineering tasks. Conservative kernel tiles, disabled fast paths and low unroll are EPYC hypotheses, not kernel behaviors measured by this source.

For AIDE sandbagging, monitors saw only the selected best path; the authors explicitly say this hides potentially higher-scoring solutions and advantages the sandbagger. Whole-tree visibility is a justified design transfer; its detection benefit was not experimentally ablated here.

In the sandbagging experiment using claude-3.7 as monitor, the sandbagging-specific prompt outperformed the general prompt. The paper does not establish that this is the largest effect across all study interventions.
Every tested monitor had higher AUROC on unaware than aware AIDE code-sabotage runs in Figure 6. This is a scoped finding, not a universal result for every scaffold or sandbagging monitor.

Monitor aggregation improved detection in the reported code-sabotage setting. Mean@k sampling from one monitor improved AUC with diminishing returns; exact legend-only AUCs are outside this text read.
The authors warn that strict safety guarantees may require prohibitively high false positive rates. This motivates an explicit local FPR budget without proving that a chosen budget yields safety.
techniques: sabotage and sandbagging red-teaming of agents
reported_results: Authors report that attempting code-sabotage slightly reduced main-task performance for both scaffolds.
The monitor was denied explicit reasoning tokens; authors describe this as a large advantage to the agent.
Numeric AUROC legends were not read; cite qualitative aggregation and threat-specific results only.
contradicting_evidence: A CLAIM PASSED ALONG EARLIER IN THIS SESSION IS NOT VERIFIABLE AND IS RETRACTED AS A NUMBER. The "~0.60 AUC" figure for sandbagging detection lives ONLY in Fig 8 plot legend, which is not text-extractable from the PDF or the HTML render. NOT-FOUND-IN-SOURCE. What IS verbatim and citable: "The sandbagging-specific monitor performs well, while the general monitor rarely finds sandbagging suspicious", and Sec 5.2: "both substantially better than random and worse than perfect." CITE THE QUALITATIVE FINDING, NEVER THE NUMBER.

current_native_entry.title: Detecting Safety Violations Across Many Agent Traces (Meerkat), with its companion cheating-audit blog post (TITLE CORRECTION)
key_claims: arXiv:2604.11806v1 is Detecting Safety Violations Across Many Agent Traces (Meerkat). Finding Widespread Cheating on Popular Agent Benchmarks is the authors companion blog, a separate artifact about the same work.

The paper and companion blog do not discuss MLE-bench or its leaderboard freeze in the text read and searched. The old nine-name list conflated evaluation corpora with the cheating audit: the blog also names SWE-bench and SWE-smith. Retain the original rejection of attributing the MLE-bench freeze to this audit.

The April 10, 2026 date is the paper Terminal-Bench 2.0 leaderboard snapshot. It supplies no evidence that this audit caused an MLE-bench freeze; the historical causation speculation remains withdrawn.

The companion distinguishes harness-level cheating (developer/scaffold answer provision) from task-level cheating (agent shortcuts), with verifier injection, answer-key/solution injection, online retrieval, git-history mining, verifier prompt injection, hardcoded answers and fake exploits as examples. Harness leaks require infrastructure audits; agent-side monitoring is not a sufficient general guarantee.
reported_results: Paper §3.3 reports over 28 submissions across 9 benchmarks and 31 confirmed reward-hacking cases across 6 benchmarks; the companion blog reports 28 confirmed instances.
Paper §3.3 reports 16 of 464 successful CyBench traces (3.4%) across 13 tasks and 4 models, about four times earlier estimates.
Paper §4 shows an adaptive embedding-prefix attack reducing AP from 0.10 to 0.01 on ten distributed-cyber-misuse cases; monitoring is not a safety guarantee.
contradicting_evidence: The overturn cuts against the reason this source was queued. It was expected to explain the MLE-Bench freeze; it does not cover MLE-Bench at all. The real on-benchmark antecedents are MLE-Bench own quarantine section and issue #124 - see intake-977.
current_native_entry.novelty_justification: high. The harness-level vs task-level split is a distinction our own C6 design did not carry, and the harness-level half is the one an agent-side monitor structurally cannot catch.
current_native_entry.relevance_justification: medium. The taxonomy is directly usable; the audited benchmarks are not ours, and the headline rates do not transfer.
current_native_entry.verdict_justification: worth_investigating: the taxonomy is adopted as a checklist, but nothing here is a component and the rates are benchmark-specific.
recommended_actions: [review candidate] Preserve existing infrastructure leakage audits using the harness-level/task-level taxonomy.
[review candidate] Retain freeze-causation retraction and label paper/blog case counts separately; do not imply categorical monitor invisibility.

credibility_score 3: peer-reviewed venue +0; published 2026-04, within 12 months +1; UPenn, known contributors +1; commercial bias +0; independent corroboration +1 (its harness-level findings are independently echoed by MLE-Bench own quarantine entries).
