current_native_entry.title: Measuring all the noises of LLM Evals — paired variance components and finite-K correction
key_claims: Wang supplies closed-form paired variance-component estimators and standard-error analysis, with data and prediction noise distinguished. Tables1-2 and Appendix A.3 are a methodology candidate, not evidence that current EPYC comparisons lack variance.

Example1 uses sqrt(2) inflation for an unpaired comparison of equally noisy model accuracies, then demonstrates reductions from pairing and repeated predictions. Faithfulness of intake-939 use is outside this source read and its existing dependency is preserved.

Appendix E relates empirical variance, question-resampling bootstrap and a paired binary win/tie/loss sign test under normal and small-effect approximations. It explicitly notes that without approximation the sign-test variance can exceed bootstrap variance; it does not prove exact universal equality or justify banning all bootstrap methods.

Finite-K correction removes bias in the described data/prediction variance decomposition. Figure5 reports about 70% RMS relative error without correction in a MATH500 experiment with K=5 and 2000 resampled questions; this is not a universal error rate for every estimator or metric.

The paper separates data noise, prediction noise and their combined total noise. Environment drift is not separately modeled here; local interleaving or drift controls need their own evidence and operator-approved measurement design, rather than an author requirement to adopt intake-939.
techniques: empirical-variance z equivalence with bootstrap and sign test
reported_results: Figure5 MATH500 uses K=5 samples per question, 1000 predictions per model/question as ground truth and bootstrapped N up to 2000; uncorrected variance-component RMS relative error is about70%.
Appendix E Eq33/36 gives binary difference variance qA+qB-(qA-qB)^2; the sign-test null uses1/2 and normal approximation requires many discordant outcomes.
contradicting_evidence: CAVEAT CONFIRMED AND IT IS DISQUALIFYING AS A CORROBORATION LEG: the author is sida@meta.com, FAIR at Meta, AND a direct SWE-RL co-author of intake-939 senior author Synnaeve. This is RESTATEMENT-CLASS SAME-LAB METHODOLOGY. It may be adopted as an instrument; it may NEVER be counted as a corroborating leg for intake-939.
Its Beta noise curves are Bernoulli-specific; our tok/s metric is continuous, so the noise model does not transfer directly to throughput measurement even where the CI machinery does.
current_native_entry.novelty_justification: high. Nothing in our measurement constitution or annexes computes a paired variance in closed form, and the small-K correction is a specific failure mode we would otherwise have hit at our typical K=3-5.
current_native_entry.relevance_justification: high. Every paired A/B we run - model ladders, kernel candidates, config arms - currently reports a point estimate with no interval.
current_native_entry.verdict_justification: adopt_patterns: closed-form noise decomposition is a useful methodology candidate within its assumptions. Statistical-method deployment remains a human-only measurement amendment; the source does not require a particular EPYC drift correction or ban resampling.
recommended_actions: [review candidate] Prepare a human-only measurement decision package for paired estimators with stated population, independence, finite-K and normal-approximation assumptions.
[review candidate] Remove the blanket prohibition on bootstrapping; AppendixE binary sign-test relation uses approximations.
[review candidate] Preserve machine-drift controls with their own evidence and intake939 dependency; do not infer an author mandate for a particular drift-correction method.
[review candidate] Keep same-lab methodology separate from independent corroboration.

current_native_entry.title: LLM test augmentation: a 61.9% per-augmentation defect rate, and a gate-before-judge hardening procedure
key_claims: The author reports SWE-bench Verified hackability 14/49 (28.5%) under iterative K=3 attacks and R2E-Gym 4/16 decisive tasks (25%) from 20 sampled tasks under K=1; these are sample-specific reported results, not independently reproduced population rates.

The author nominates 65 failures among 105 decisive generated-test sanity checks (61.9%) as the central methodology finding. This per-augmentation rate is distinct from 14/49 task-level hackability and specific to the11-task repair experiment.

The proposed hardening loop injects a generated test into the real project test file, applies gold and runs the native runner; failures are discarded and retried before a3-sample self-consistency judge receives accepted tests.

In a stratified eight-pair Docker re-verification, the LLM judge had endorsed all six named INVALID_AUG tests as BLOCKS even though they failed gold sanity. This is a bounded failure demonstration, not a universal judge error rate.

The reported11-task ablation reaches3 upgrades without retry and9 with either diversity-biased or neutral retry. Retry presence dominated this small experiment; equivalent totals do not prove retry style irrelevant generally.

current_native_entry.verdict_justification: adopt_patterns: the procedure transfers and is cheap; the code is not open and cannot be a component.

current_native_entry.title: Performance-Aligned LLMs for Generating Fast HPC Code — stored-reference reward ratio and branch geometry
key_claims: The read arXiv v1 uses PPO with a KL penalty, direct runtime reward for CodeContests and a learned reward for synthetic problems, and reports a synthetic-data ablation. No binary-versus-continuous reward ablation was found in the read reward-method and synthetic-data-ablation sections to settle compatibility with intake-939; that comparison needs the other primary source.

Publisher-deposited Crossref metadata confirms Performance-Aligned LLMs for Generating Fast HPC Code in IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems, June2026, DOI10.1109/TPDS.2026.3675550. Mechanistic claims here are anchored to the available2024 arXiv v1, not assumed identical journal text.

The CodeContests reward uses a median runtime from submissions already in the collected dataset divided by generated-code runtime. Collection used a single EPYC7763 core. This creates a stored-reference comparison hazard, but the read text does not establish isolated load, a contemporaneous denominator, or exact runtime measurement placement on the training node.

Eq4 assigns incorrect CodeContests code -1 and correct code M/t-1; for positive M,t the gap to -1 is M/t and vanishes as t tends to infinity, not near t=M. The synthetic branch is a learned reward and has no explicit executable correctness branch in Eq4; this does not prove absence of every validation mechanism.

The authors report improved pass@1 for fine-tuned models and attribute this to more training data and, for RLPF/DPA, negative rewards from incorrect samples. This is their explanation, not a causal ablation isolating that mechanism.

The Generator-Validator Agent System
Figure 2

Generator-Validator Agents Pipeline.
(a) The Generator Agent writes a generator program and generator commands to produce test cases. (b) The Validator Agent writes a validator program to check if the test cases satisfy all the constraints stated in the problem. Test cases that fail validation, along with specific comments provided by the validator program, are then fed back to the Generator Agent for revision.
To simultaneously address the challenges of correctness and coverage in test case construction, we propose a Generator-Validator agent system. The Generator agent is an LLM-based agent that writes test input generators based on the problem description. The Validator agent is also an LLM agent that writes test input validators to supervise the Generator agent, ensuring that the test input generated by the Generator agent conforms to the problem constraints. This agent system can automatically build a large-scale and rigorous dataset for LLM training by leveraging publicly available data such as problem statements and ground truth solutions. An overview of the workflow is presented in Fig.
2
. Specific implementation details for the generator and validator are presented below.
3.1
Generator
Generator Program.
The generator program accepts input data conditions, such as data size and characteristics, via command-line arguments. It then generates a piece of input data that conforms to these specified conditions. This generated input data is then fed into the ground truth solution to produce outputs and hence form a complete set of test cases. The advantage of this design is that a single generator program, combined with varying command-line arguments, can generate a diverse range of test cases. A generator demo is presented in Appendix
9.2
.
Agent Workflow.
Initially, the Generator Agent is given a problem statement. It is then instructed to read the statement carefully, and identify, and summarize the constraints of the input data. Subsequently, the Generator Agent will analyze the problem to anticipate potential mistakes contestants might make and identify possible corner cases. Based on this analysis, it will design targeted adversarial test cases. Finally, the Generator Agent will synthesize all of this information to produce a compliant generator program. Since it is up to the agent to determine which command-line arguments the generator program needs to receive, we also require the agent to provide approximately 20 commands. These commands should cover a range of data sizes, from small to large, and all relevant special types. We will then execute these commands to finally obtain the test input.

Scalability.

Test cases serve to determine the correctness of a given code. Therefore, we treat code evaluation as a binary classification problem. This approach allows us to evaluate the test cases themselves as binary classifiers, assessing their ability to distinguish between correct and incorrect solutions accurately. By doing so, we can objectively and rigorously evaluate the quality of test cases within a code dataset, including their coverage and correctness. To our knowledge, CodeContests
+
is the first dataset project to conduct such rigorous validation of test case accuracy. We believe this level of evaluation is crucial for establishing a dataset’s trustworthiness.
Data.
CodeContests has collected tens of millions of submissions, each with a “correct”/“incorrect” label. We sampled 100 positive samples (correct submissions) and 100 negative samples (incorrect submissions) for each problem. For problems without sufficient samples, we included as many available submissions as possible. In this way, we selected 10,166 problems that contained at least 10 positive and negative samples, as well as a corresponding 1.72 million submissions. We used these problems and samples to evaluate the accuracy of the test cases in CodeContests
+
and CodeContests.
Engineering.
Since each submission needs to be evaluated on approximately 200 test cases on average, the total number of program executions is more than 300 million. We implemented a cloud architecture for such large-scale evaluation, running on a cluster with 25,000 CPU cores and 70 TB memory, and completed the experiment on this platform. Some engineering details are presented in Appendix
8
.

We use True Positive Rate (TPR) and True Negative Rate (TNR) to quantitatively assess accuracy. TPR measures the ability of test cases to correctly classify positive instances (correct solutions), thus reflecting the test case’s correctness. This is because if a test case satisfies all the problem’s constraints, a correct solution should not be misclassified as incorrect. Therefore, a low TPR primarily indicates that the test case itself is flawed. TNR measures the ability of test cases to correctly classify negative instances (incorrect solutions) as incorrect, thereby primarily reflecting the test case’s coverage. Overly simplistic test cases may fail to identify errors in incorrect code, leading to false positives (i.e., incorrect solutions being deemed correct).

current_native_entry.title: Honest Lying: Understanding Memory Confabulation in Reflexive Agents
key_claims: The authors report a memory-wipe comparison in 16 selected frozen ALFWorld environments: env_31 and env_97 solve in 1 trial without memory versus 7 and 8 in original Reflexion logs (+6/+7 trials); 14 fail within the 10-trial no-memory budget. This is bounded author-reported evidence that memory can harm, not 2/16 trials or proven independent corroboration. Original Reflexion logs use a 15-trial budget, whereas all mitigation conditions use 10 trials. Section 5.3 says standard Reflexion solves none within 10, despite §4.4 and Table 2 reporting original-log TTS of 7 and 8 for env_31 and env_97. This source-internal budget and result tension is unresolved; the comparison does not establish a controlled same-budget causal magnitude.

The paper proposes a write-path confabulation hypothesis under binary feedback and persistent reflection retrieval, supported by named wrong-object reflections and mitigation comparisons. It does not experimentally isolate write-side from read-side failure or establish a distinct fourth causal mechanism.

In 16 frozen environments selected from 50 reflection-requiring ALFWorld environments in 134 original logs, zero of 121 reflections mention the target object extracted from the gamefile name. In env_22 all 14 reflections reference tomato/microwave instead of Mug/CoffeeMachine; this mention proxy is not a complete semantic correctness test.

RRR is passive post-hoc redundancy measurement: for reflections after the first, count those having SequenceMatcher similarity≥0.85 to any earlier reflection and divide by |M|−1; RRR≥0.5 labels frozen memory. The proposed feedback parser extracts Nothing happens responses and repeated-action loops before an LLM still explains failures and writes a plan; this is not prospective rejection or removal of model diagnosis.

small sample limits statistical power. Similarly, the HumanEval
analysis covers only 4 frozen problems, making the cross-domain
parallel structurally consistent but underpowered compared to the ALFWorld analysis (16 environments, 121 reflections). Our
operational definition uses target-object mention as the
grounding signal for detecting confabulation, which is a
sufficient but not necessary condition: a reflection could
mention the correct object while still misdiagnosing the failure
cause, or confabulate in dimensions we do not measure such as
wrong location or wrong action sequence. Finally, all experiments
use pre-existing logs from the public Reflexion repository,
fixing the model backbone (gpt-3.5-turbo), environment version,
and hyperparameters; results may differ under other
configurations.
